research:
  - id: exit-paper
    topic: State Development
    title: "Mass Exit in the Market for Governance"
    status: "R&R, *International Organization*"
    pdf: "files/exit_paper.pdf"
    abstract: >-
      State development theories posit political fragmentation lets subjects exit to other authorities, spurring jurisdictional competition that drives institutional development, yet behavioral evidence remains scarce. I develop a theory of exit under horizontal and vertical authority and test it in Tokugawa Japan’s distinctive setting. Across nearly 300 domains, villages sought concessions from home rulers by fleeing en masse or appealing through neighboring lords or to the central authority. I use domain conversions to central rule as a natural experiment: they brought central authority closer to neighboring villages. Difference-in-differences analysis finds 3.9 percentage points more exit among nearby villages under other lords, without detectable changes in confrontation. Grid-year panel data show proximity to another ruler’s capital predicted more exit but not confrontation. Proximity to neighboring capitals predicted lower reported tax rates where neighboring domains could absorb more migrants. These findings suggest fragmentation helps translate overlapping jurisdictions into popular checks on elite power.

  - id: verification-paper
    topic: Cognitive Warfare
    title: "Verifying Away Collective Knowledge"
    status: Under review
    pdf: "files/verification_paper.pdf"
    abstract: >-
      Generative AI lets influence operations fabricate apparent widespread
      support cheaply. I develop a theoretical framework for online forums
      involving politically restricted information to isolate a tradeoff
      between authenticity and accuracy that generative AI exacerbates.
      Citizens collectively choose verification, then decide among anonymous
      posting, verified posting, and silence. When attackers can flood
      anonymous forums, citizens adopt the least verification that deters
      them. Because greater access raises knowledge and exposure,
      verification exposes better-informed sources to greater punishment risk
      and, unlike in canonical screening models, excludes the best-informed,
      hence most strongly motivated to contribute, first. Citizens value
      collective accuracy, but individual contributions remain externalities;
      private exposure risk therefore makes the forum more authentic but less
      informative, allowing the influence operation to deplete collective
      knowledge without deployment or deception. Detection and per-post costs
      reduce reliance on identity verification. Evaluations of epistemic
      security should track both the fakes excluded and the composition of
      who remains.

  - id: assurance-paper
    topic: Interstate Conflict
    title: "Modern Force and Coercive Backfire"
    status: Working paper
    pdf: "files/assurance_paper.pdf"
    abstract: >-
      Modern military technologies, including automated weapons and AI-assisted
      systems, are thought to strengthen deterrence and preserve peace by enhancing
      limited military operations without provoking wider war. I challenge this
      optimism by examining their implications for coercive bargaining rather than
      their direct military effects. I develop a coercive bargaining model with a *subwar capability*:
      access to limited operations short of general war. Such operations can replace
      war after resistance or settlement after compliance, potentially weakening
      coercive threats and assurances. The target may concede less, further weakening
      assurances and the government's ability to secure concessions. Across broad
      parameter regions, I show that subwar capability can lower coercive ability and
      increase war, even when no operation is used. Subwar capability can weaken the
      effect of military power on coercive ability and reduce social welfare by
      raising conflict costs. More efficient military technology can thus disrupt coercive
      bargaining and raise the cost of conflict.

  - id: attack-option-paper
    topic: Interstate Conflict
    title: "Assurance in Coercive Bargaining"
    coauthors: "[Shuhei Kurizaki](https://skurizaki.github.io/)"
    status: Working paper
    pdf: "files/attack_option_paper.pdf"
    abstract: >-
      Political actors can fail to secure concessions despite credible threats when
      targets fear that yielding could invite further harm. We show that this assurance
      problem can complicate signaling through coercive demands, making it harder for
      targets to distinguish restraint from plans to attack. Our bargaining model allows
      concessions to improve the demanding state's military position before it decides
      whether to attack. This gives states planning an attack a reason to imitate the
      modest demands of states seeking peace. Greater military strength can make
      reassuring demand patterns harder to sustain and permit additional ways to conceal
      an intended attack. These changes can reduce the concessions the demanding state
      obtains peacefully and increase the risk of war, imposing collective costs when
      disputes that could have been settled peacefully instead lead to fighting. Lack of
      assurance can exacerbate information problems in interstate politics, undermining
      coercive bargaining and making peace harder to secure.

```{=html}
<div class="abstract-overlay" id="abstract-overlay" hidden>
  <div class="abstract-modal" role="dialog" aria-modal="true" aria-labelledby="abstract-modal-title" tabindex="-1">
    <button class="abstract-modal-close" type="button" aria-label="Close">&#10005;</button>
    <span class="abstract-modal-topic" id="abstract-modal-topic"></span>
    <span class="abstract-modal-title" id="abstract-modal-title"></span>
    <div class="abstract-modal-body" id="abstract-modal-body"></div>
  </div>
</div>

<script>
window.addEventListener("DOMContentLoaded", function () {
  const overlay = document.getElementById("abstract-overlay");
  if (!overlay) return;

  const topicEl = document.getElementById("abstract-modal-topic");
  const titleEl = document.getElementById("abstract-modal-title");
  const bodyEl = document.getElementById("abstract-modal-body");
  const closeBtn = overlay.querySelector(".abstract-modal-close");
  let lastTrigger = null;

  const closeModal = () => {
    overlay.hidden = true;
    document.body.classList.remove("abstract-open");
    if (lastTrigger) {
      lastTrigger.setAttribute("aria-expanded", "false");
      lastTrigger.focus();
      lastTrigger = null;
    }
  };

  document.querySelectorAll(".pub-abstract-btn").forEach((btn) => {
    btn.addEventListener("click", function (event) {
      event.preventDefault();
      const entry = btn.closest(".pub-entry");
      if (!entry) return;
      const abstract = entry.querySelector(".pub-abstract");
      if (!abstract) return;

      const topic = entry.querySelector(".pub-topic");
      const title = entry.querySelector(".pub-title");
      topicEl.textContent = topic ? topic.textContent : "";
      topicEl.hidden = !topic;
      titleEl.innerHTML = title ? title.innerHTML : "";
      bodyEl.innerHTML = abstract.innerHTML;

      lastTrigger = btn;
      btn.setAttribute("aria-expanded", "true");
      overlay.hidden = false;
      document.body.classList.add("abstract-open");
      const modal = overlay.querySelector(".abstract-modal");
      modal.scrollTop = 0;
      modal.focus();
    });
  });

  document.querySelectorAll(".pub-abstract-btn").forEach((btn) => {
    btn.addEventListener("keydown", function (event) {
      if (event.key === " " || event.key === "Spacebar") {
        event.preventDefault();
        btn.click();
      }
    });
  });

  closeBtn.addEventListener("click", closeModal);

  overlay.addEventListener("click", function (event) {
    if (event.target === overlay) closeModal();
  });

  document.addEventListener("keydown", function (event) {
    if (event.key === "Escape" && !overlay.hidden) closeModal();
  });
});
</script>
```
